english.html: He who first joined me to himself took my loves away with him; let him keep them with him, and guard them in the tomb (Ille meos primus, qui me sibi iunxit, amores / abstulit: ille habeat secum, servetque sepulchro).

we should have no great trouble in settling this question. But since not all have such a gift of continence, nor the power to tame and vanquish with such great strength the passion of the flesh, and since after the husband's death God by His holy law permits every woman to remarry whom she will <sup class="mk" data-key="p">p</sup>: I say, to the point of our question, that although the civil law in one place was content to make the wife wait five years <sup class="mk" data-key="q">q</sup>, nevertheless the Emperor Justinian and the Pontiffs of Rome have willed that, even though thirty years had passed, if there is no certain news of the husband, it is not lawful for the wife to remarry <sup class="mk" data-key="r">r</sup>. True it is that the same authors well intend that the news shall be found certain enough (the husband having died in the war) if the captain under whom the husband followed arms sent a certificate of his death, or himself in person attested it <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>. Or else, if the husband was drowned, by proving that the ship in which he was has foundered. Indeed it would suffice to show by witnesses, or otherwise, that the rumour of his death is spread abroad everywhere <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>. For although proof by rumour and common repute, according to the ordinary and common rules, is not conclusive, nor received <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>, nevertheless, where one cannot easily obtain true and certain proof, as when the husband had remained in a distant country, long absent, such a manner of proof, by rumour and repute, would suffice <sup class="mk" data-key="y">y</sup>.

notes.gloss: A widow "is at liberty to be married to whom she will."

notes.citation: Digest 24.2.6 (De divortiis, l. Uxores); Novel 22 (De nuptiis, coll. 4), § Sed etiam (cf. Nov. 22 c. 6, the five-year wait for the spouse of a captive)

notes.gloss: Justinian abrogates the old four-year rule: a soldier's wife may not remarry, however long the silence, without certification of his death; the decretal applies the same rule.
